rationale: The hypothesis posits that PLAA variants account for approximately 1-2% of atypical or genetic cerebral palsy (CP) cohorts. While PLAA is recognized as a CP mimic causing progressive microcephaly, spastic quadriparesis, and leukoencephalopathy (OMIM #617527) and has been included on CP gene panels (such as PanelApp and diagnostic panels), the quantitative claim of a 1-2% prevalence is not supported by systematic cohort studies. The single atypical CP cohort in the literature that identified a PLAA variant (Han et al., 2025) evaluated only 10 patients, yielding 1/10 (10%), which suffers from profound small-sample ascertainment bias and cannot substantiate a generalized 1-2% prevalence rate across broader atypical CP cohorts. Given that PLAA-associated neurodevelopmental disorder is an ultra-rare autosomal recessive condition characterized by progressive infantile neurodegeneration rather than static motor encephalopathy, extrapolating a fixed 1-2% incidence in CP mimics lacks empirical validation.

evidence.text: In a cohort of 10 Korean patients with atypical cerebral palsy, whole exome and/or genome sequencing identified likely pathogenic or pathogenic variants in 6 genes, including one individual harboring a PLAA variant (1/10 or 10% in this small cohort).

source.title: Genetic alterations in atypical cerebral palsy identified through chromosomal microarray and exome sequencing
source.quote: This study investigated the genetic causes of atypical cerebral palsy (CP) through chromosomal microarray (CMA) and exome sequencing (ES) in a cohort of 10 Korean patients to identify variants and expand the spectrum of mutations associated with atypical cerebral palsy... six likely pathogenic variants (LPVs) or pathogenic variants (PVs) detected in the SLC2A1, PLAA, CDC42BPB, CACNA1D, ALG12, and SACS genes (n = 6).

evidence.text: PLAA mutations were characterized in seven patients from consanguineous pedigrees presenting with progressive microcephaly, spastic quadriparesis, and global developmental delay associated with a novel form of leukoencephalopathy, rather than static cerebral palsy.

source.title: Phospholipase A2-activating protein is associated with a novel form of leukoencephalopathy
source.quote: Herein, we have identified a unique form of leukoencephalopathy in seven patients presenting at ages 2 to 4 months with progressive microcephaly, spastic quadriparesis, and global developmental delay... The novel phenotype of our patients segregated with a homozygous loss-of-function sequence variant, causing the substitution of leucine at position 752 to phenylalanine, in PLAA

conflicts: Han et al. (2025) identified a PLAA variant in 1 of 10 patients (10%) in a highly selected atypical CP cohort, which contradicts the proposed 1-2% population estimate due to extreme sample size limitation and selection bias.

PLAA-related disorder represents an ultra-rare progressive neurodegenerative leukoencephalopathy/microcephaly syndrome; large CP sequencing initiatives do not identify PLAA at a recurrent 1-2% frequency.

new_directions.question_text: What is the true diagnostic yield of PLAA pathogenic variants across large, multi-center prospective cohorts (>1,000 patients) with clinically diagnosed CP or CP mimics?
new_directions.rationale: Existing data in atypical CP are restricted to a pilot study of 10 patients; large unselected cohorts are required to measure accurate frequency.

new_directions.question_text: Can neuroimaging biomarkers (specific leukoencephalopathy patterns and cerebellar atrophy) reliably distinguish PLAA-related progressive disorder from non-progressive spastic-dyskinetic CP in early infancy?
new_directions.rationale: Because PLAA manifests with rapid postnatal microcephaly and white matter degradation, early neuroimaging discriminators could avoid misclassification as static hypoxic-ischemic or dyskinetic CP.
